opus-5.5.text:
Reproducibility is one of those problems that sits at a really nice sweet spot. On one hand, it matters a lot. There's been a lot of hand-wringing about the reproducibility crisis across many fields, and even in computational research, where you'd think things should be straightforward because the code and data are supposedly right there, it turns out that a surprisingly large fraction of papers can't be reproduced without a lot of effort. Dependencies are missing, the instructions are incomplete, versions have changed, things break. So there's real value in automating that.

On the other hand, it's a well-defined task in a way that a lot of the grand visions for AI in science aren't. People talk about AI agents doing autonomous research, coming up with novel hypotheses, and so on, and it's very hard to evaluate whether an agent is actually doing that well. With reproducibility, you have a paper, you have the code and data, and the question is: can you run it and get the results the authors reported? There's a ground truth. That makes it something you can actually build a rigorous benchmark around, which is what we tried to do with CORE-Bench.

And I think it's a necessary stepping stone. If agents can't reliably reproduce existing work, which is in some sense the most basic, unglamorous part of science, then we should be pretty skeptical of claims that they're about to automate the creative parts. Conversely, if they get good at it, that's genuinely useful today. It's tedious work that researchers and reviewers don't have time to do, so it mostly doesn't get done. An agent that could check whether a paper's results reproduce, at scale, could meaningfully improve the quality of the scientific literature.

The last thing I'd say is that it's a great lens on what agents actually struggle with. It's not usually deep reasoning. It's the messy, real-world stuff: navigating a file system, figuring out which version of a library to install, recovering when something fails, knowing when to give up on one approach and try another. Those are exactly the capabilities that matter for agents to be useful in practice, so it's a good test of whether the hype matches reality.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts reproducibility with ambitious AI research that is hard to evaluate, but it does not clearly state that solving abstract reasoning alone has uncertain practical payoff.

r002.rationale: It calls reproducibility a stepping stone before automating creative work, but does not say reproducing a paper’s results is a prerequisite for building on that paper.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether failures to reproduce code are caused by cheating.

r004.rationale: It mentions that software versions change and may need to be identified, but does not state that slight version differences can substantially change research outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reproducibility is interesting for a couple of reasons, and they pull in slightly different directions.

The first is that it's a genuinely important problem. We've written a lot about the reproducibility crisis in machine learning-based science, where you have papers across dozens of fields claiming impressive predictive performance, and when you look closely there's data leakage, or the test set isn't really held out, or the baseline is misspecified. The result is a scientific literature that's much less reliable than it looks. And the bottleneck for fixing that is human labor. Reproducing a paper is tedious. Nobody gets tenure for doing it. So if agents could take on even a meaningful fraction of that work, that's real value, not a demo.

The second reason is more about what it tells us about agents themselves. Reproducibility is a nice benchmark task because it has a lot of the messiness of real work. You're reading a paper written by someone who didn't anticipate your questions, you're dealing with code that may or may not match the paper, data that has to be found and cleaned, environments that have to be set up. There's no single correct answer you can pattern-match to. At the same time, there is a ground truth: either you get the result or you don't, and you can check how far off you are. That combination of open-ended process and verifiable outcome is pretty rare, and it's exactly what you want if you're trying to measure whether agents can do substantive work rather than just pass a multiple-choice test.

And the third thing I'd say is that it's a case where the failure modes are relatively safe. If an agent gets a reproduction wrong, it wastes some compute and maybe produces a wrong report that a human then has to check. That's a very different risk profile from an agent that's booking your travel or moving money around. So it's a domain where we can actually learn what agents are good at and where they fall down, in a setting where the stakes of being wrong are bounded.

What we found when we actually looked at this is that the agents are not nearly as capable as the marketing suggests. They can handle the mechanical parts reasonably well, but the moment a reproduction requires judgment, like realizing the paper's description is ambiguous and deciding what the authors probably meant, they tend to either guess confidently or quietly give up. And that gap between what's advertised and what's delivered is, in some ways, the most useful thing the task reveals.

r001.rationale: The response presents reproducibility as a valuable, verifiable agent task, but does not contrast it with the uncertain payoff of solving abstract reasoning alone.

r002.rationale: It discusses reproducing papers but does not say reproduction is a prerequisite for building on their findings.

r003.rationale: It mentions data leakage and flawed baselines, but does not state that reproduction failures are rarely due to cheating.

r004.rationale: It mentions setting up environments, but does not explain how small software library version differences can substantially change research outputs.

astra-6.text:
Scientific reproducibility is a useful test for AI agents because it requires more than producing a plausible answer. You have a paper, perhaps some code and data, and a concrete question: Can you actually reproduce the reported result? An agent has to work through the details—setting up the environment, understanding the analysis, figuring out what’s missing—and check whether the evidence supports the conclusion.

That gives us a way to evaluate agents on meaningful scientific work. Did they reproduce the result? If they couldn’t, did they correctly identify why? A dependency problem is very different from a finding that doesn’t hold up, and we want agents to distinguish those cases rather than confidently declare success or failure.

There’s also a direct benefit to science. Reproduction takes time, and researchers don’t always get much credit for doing it. If agents can reduce that burden, even with human oversight, we could make checking results a much more routine part of research.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility a meaningful test for agents, but does not contrast it with the uncertain practical payoff of solving abstract reasoning alone.

r002.rationale: It describes checking whether a reported result can be reproduced, but does not say reproduction is a prerequisite for building on the paper.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss cheating as a cause of failures to reproduce scientific code.

r004.rationale: It mentions dependency problems generally, but does not explain that slight software library version differences can substantially change research outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
Scientific reproducibility is a useful test for AI agents because it involves a lot of the messy work that real research requires. You’re not just answering a question about a paper. You have to understand what the authors did, find the code and data, get the environment working, run the experiments, and figure out whether the results support the claims.

That requires sustained reasoning and interaction with tools, but it also gives you something concrete to check. Did you reproduce the result? If you didn’t, can you explain why? A failed reproduction doesn’t necessarily mean the paper is wrong; it could be a missing detail, a different experimental setup, or a mistake by the agent. Making those distinctions is part of the challenge.

And the work is valuable in its own right. Even an agent that helps with some of those steps could reduce the effort required for researchers to check and build on each other’s work.

r001.rationale: The response calls reproducibility a concrete test for agents, but does not contrast it with the uncertain practical payoff of solving abstract reasoning alone.

r002.rationale: It says agents could help researchers check and build on each other’s work, but does not state that reproducing a paper’s reported results is a prerequisite for building on it.

r003.rationale: The response discusses possible reasons for reproduction failures, but does not say failures are rarely due to cheating.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention software library versions or their effect on research outputs.
